The backstory is that over a lot of years, what became increasingly apparent is that where the rest of the world would pay a lot of attention to a missing, you know, white person. that didn't get the same reaction for Native American people. And so there was and continues to be a huge backlog of cold cases involving missing and murdered Indigenous people for which their families have never been given an opportunity to tell their story or to have their story heard. And so in keeping with kind of the work that I've been doing to try and bring, I think, a greater sense of security to the reservations. We introduced Lisa Murkowski and I introduced a bill that we called Savannah's Act after Savannah Gray win. That act almost got passed in the Congress, last Congress, and I'm hoping it'll get passed in this Congress. It's really modest, it's just a first step. turn_text: You said another thing that I thought was really interesting in your talk today was that violating principles of sovereignty is a big problem in Washington and I think that in the upper great plains you hear about the concept of sovereignty but it's really theoretical. You might not totally understand why it matters the type of impact that it has then day to day in native communities. Why does sovereignty matter and why is sovereignty important towards maybe taking the next critical steps of providing these communities with better resources or even a decision-making model that they can use than to improve their communities?

I would put it this way. If the state of North Dakota would only have half of its sovereignty, it'd only be half as effective in protecting its citizens. I think you've got to put this in the context of any other sovereign entity, whether it's a state, whether it's a county, whether it's a city. And you have to think about how, in many cases, tribal officials are really hampered in what they can do. But I also think that Washington, here's a great example of not understanding tribal sovereignty. If you ask people in Congress why there is Indian gaming, you know what they say? Because we allowed it. You know what the real answer is? They restricted it. The real answer is the Supreme Court said Native Americans as sovereign entities can decide whether they're going to have gambling on the reservations. And then Congress intervened to restrict the kinds of games to restrict and require that Native Americans seek approval from the states. So I think if you told that story, if you told the story of what happened with Indian gaming, people would be shocked because they think Indian gaming is something that they allowed as opposed to what they regulated and curtailed.
